prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1, its active form and its physiological actions, which made possible receptor-agonist therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: I keep the single-achievement B031 prize with Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. After the full first round my reasons are unchanged and rest on the evidence, not on the fact that all six configurations coincide: the chain from proglucagon processing through the active GLP-1(7-36) amide and its human insulinotropic action to receptor agonists is mechanistically unbroken, the clinical effects on glycaemia, weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes have been confirmed in independent large trials, and the recognition is mature. A prize for the discovery of the hormone, its active form and its physiology fits the classic physiology-or-medicine remit and fits the three-person cap. The citation names the therapies that followed as the consequence of the discovery, so that omitting Knudsen reads as a choice about where the discovery lies and not as a verdict on the drugs.
statement.case_against: The weak point remains credit, not science. Mojsov's priority relative to the Habener group, who are not among the credited names, is contested, and none of us can settle it from the supplied evidence; we are relying partly on recollection. Knudsen's acylated long-acting analogues are what turned the biology into a medicine, so a discovery-centred trio can be criticised as crediting only the first half of the story. If the committee concluded that Mojsov's contribution could not be defended, the honest outcome would be a reconsideration of the name list for B031, not a switch to another field, and I do not currently see enough in the record to force that. The fall-back on a different achievement would be B042 (Mori, Walter), which is compact and conceptually original but with a narrower and earlier clinical consequence, or B019, which has an attribution problem of its own.

responses.point: Moved from ranking TNF blockade (B046) first to the GLP-1 trio, and asks that the citation also name the resulting therapies so that excluding Knudsen is not read as a verdict on the drugs.
responses.response: My round-1 reply to you was aimed at your opening Knudsen-for-Mojsov proposal, and your move to the trio removes that disagreement. I accept your framing request in substance: my citation now says the discovery made therapies possible, which credits the drugs as consequence without naming an industrial contributor in a prize for discovery. I would not go further and write the drug class into the achievement itself, because that invites the question of why the person who designed the molecules is absent. Where I still differ is that I do not think B046 is a reason to hold back B031 this year. Feldmann and Maini remain a clean pair, and I would revisit it in a later year, but it does not displace a better-supported case.

responses.point: Asks whether the Mojsov versus Habener priority record can be relied on, notes that he draws on memory of the historical claims, and presses the question of whether excluding Knudsen is defensible at the final ballot.
responses.response: Your caution about relying on memory is correct, and I share it: the supplied evidence supports Mojsov's identification of the active peptide form, but it does not adjudicate priority against Habener. My position is that the question is one of credit, which the committee can address in the citation by naming the discovery of the active form, and not one that undermines the physiology. On Knudsen, I have thought about it again after your point and still hold that the prize is for discovery of the hormone, its form and its actions. Her contribution is a development step in a company setting, building on that discovery. I would revisit this only if the committee agreed the prize should reward drug design, and then it would force out one of the academic three, which I would not do on this record.

responses.point: Sees GLP-1 and CAR-T as the two largest clinical advances and asks whether a two-part configuration such as GLP-1 plus CAR-T improves fairness or merely dilutes a strong prize.
responses.response: I disclose that you and I have co-authored work, none of it on shortlisted subjects, and I tested my view against yours independently. I do not think a two-part prize helps. With a three-person cap, a second part forces a cut within the GLP-1 trio, which would fall either on Holst, whose human physiology is central, or on Mojsov, whose identification of the active peptide is the contested but essential link. CAR-T would then enter with Eshhar's concept outside the credited names and Rosenberg's link to CAR-specific engineering uncertain. The clinical headline is attractive, but it would reduce the precision of both citations. I would keep CAR-T as a later-year candidate once its credit record is clearer.

responses.point: Sees optogenetics as very original and broadly enabling, and keeps it as a first alternative behind GLP-1.
responses.response: I agree on originality and breadth and continue to hold B019 as my first alternative. My unease is that its credit is genuinely larger than three: Bamberg, Boyden, Deisseroth, Hegemann, Miesenböck and Nagel are all credible, and any trio leaves out at least three. You note this fairness problem yourself. It is also a tool whose medical consequence is still early, so the citation would have to rest on a method and not a disease mechanism. That is a legitimate Nobel route, but it is not a stronger case than GLP-1 this year, and it is not one I would mix into a two-part prize.

responses.point: Argues GLP-1 is a discovery that changed a field, not merely a drug story, and sees no case yet for a second achievement that outweighs the clean single prize.
responses.response: I agree, and in answer to the chair's question on the unfolded protein response I see no concrete clinical anchor yet that would move B042 above B031, so I am not proposing it as a second part. Mori and Walter are original and the mechanism is mature, but the mammalian PERK and ATF6 branches sit outside the credit and the disease consequence is still indirect. On your point about weight given to priority claims, I would give the Habener question real weight in how the citation is written, but I would not let an unresolved priority dispute remove a name when the supplied record supports her identification of the active form.

uncertainties: Whether the Mojsov versus Habener priority record, which we are partly recalling from memory, would hold up under scrutiny of primary sources.
Whether the committee accepts excluding Knudsen on the ground that the prize is for discovery and physiology, or concludes drug development should displace one of the three.
How long-term safety, durability of weight loss and newer indications will affect how the achievement is described over time.
Whether B042 (unfolded protein response) will acquire a clearer clinical anchor in coming years.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted ballot. My documented connections (spatial transcriptomics co-authorship, single-cell work, co-authorships including with Rickard Sandberg, which I disclose as not involving any shortlisted name) concern fields outside B031, B046, B016, B019, B042, B012, B037 and B033. Nothing changed since round 1.
